cards.title: Read PageSpeed Insights: Field Data (CrUX) vs Lab Data (Lighthouse)
cards.summary: PageSpeed Insights shows two separate reports — 28-day real-user CrUX field data and simulated Lighthouse lab data — and you optimize against the lab half.
cards.use_when: Interpreting a PageSpeed Insights report for a product page, category page, or homepage and deciding which numbers to trust when setting speed work priorities.
steps: Open pagespeed.web.dev (verify the current interface) and enter the URL of the store page you want to assess.
Keep the toggle on Mobile. The source's focus is always mobile because most web browsing happens on phones, not because mobile is harder.
Read the top section as field data: anonymized Chrome UX Report (CrUX) data aggregated over the past 28 days from real Chrome users on that URL. This is what real shoppers experienced.
Read the second section as lab data (Lighthouse): a simulation of a mid-tier device on a mobile network, run once, used for immediate diagnostic feedback.
Expect the two sections to disagree — the source shows LCP of 1.6s in field data vs 1.1s FCP in lab data on the same page. That does not mean one is wrong.
Prioritize fixing lab data issues, because improvements there eventually surface in field data, but expect a roughly 28-day lag before the field numbers reflect your work.
If you are failing Core Web Vitals but lab looks clean, the cause is real-user conditions (device mix, network, third-party scripts), not a reporting error.
caveats: Field data needs enough Chrome traffic in the 28-day window; low-traffic pages show no URL data at all.
Lab data measures Total Blocking Time, not First Input Delay — FID only exists in field data because it requires real interactions.

cards.title: Use the Origin vs URL toggle to read low-traffic page speed
cards.summary: When a specific page lacks enough traffic for CrUX data, PageSpeed Insights blocks the URL view and shows the site-wide average instead.
cards.use_when: Auditing speed on a new product page, a low-traffic landing page, or a niche category page and wondering why the field data does not match what you expect for that page.
steps: Look at the URL/Origin toggle in the field data section after running the test.
Notice whether the URL option is greyed out — if it is, the specific page did not receive enough Chrome traffic in the past 28 days.
Accept the Origin figure as the site-wide average across all pages, and read it as a general health signal, not a diagnosis of that page.
Use lab data for that page instead: it runs on every URL regardless of traffic and gives you page-specific issues to fix.
If the whole site lacks traffic for 28 days, no field data will appear at all — work entirely from lab data until volume builds.
Track the Origin trend over weeks as a proxy for site-wide speed health on lower-traffic stores.
caveats: Origin data blends your fastest and slowest pages, so a single broken template can hide inside a healthy average.
The 28-day window means recent fixes will not show up immediately.

cards.title: Fix LCP by identifying the largest element and optimizing it
cards.summary: LCP measures how long the largest above-the-fold element takes to load; identify that element in lab diagnostics, then optimize it by type.
cards.use_when: Improving page speed on a product page or homepage where the hero image, banner, or headline is the first thing shoppers see.
steps: Treat LCP under 2.5s as good (green), 2.5–4.0s as needs improvement (orange), and over 4.0s as poor (red) — these are the thresholds the source states.
Find the LCP element: in lab data, expand Diagnostics and open 'Largest Contentful Paint element' to see exactly what it is (image, video, or text block).
If it is an image: resize to the dimensions actually rendered, compress the file below roughly 250KB, and serve in a modern format such as WebP or AVIF.
If it is a video: compress the file to reduce its size.
If it is text: leave it. The source's opinion is that a text LCP is the fastest-loading option, so prefer a text-led hero when design allows.
Remember that a slow LCP is usually not a web server problem — the source attributes it mainly to your theme, plugins, and the page elements you placed.
caveats: The 250KB image guidance and text-LCP preference are the source's recommendations, not vendor-published requirements.
The 1,200px recommended image width mentioned in the source is tied to Google Discover eligibility, not LCP itself.

cards.title: Fix CLS on checkout and product pages with reserved space and image dimensions
cards.summary: CLS measures how far elements shift after load; on an ecommerce page it can cause a shopper to tap the wrong quantity or button.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing layout jumps on a cart, checkout, or product page where shoppers mis-tap quantities, variants, or the place-order button.
steps: Read the score as: 0.1 or less good, 0.1–0.25 needs improvement, above 0.25 poor — the thresholds the source states.
Remember the source's illustration: a shopper on the checkout page who casually selects 56 items by accident is the result of a layout shift moving the control under their finger.
Audit the page for dynamically injected content — ads, embeds, iframes — that loads after the initial render and pushes content down.

For each such element, reserve a dedicated placeholder with fixed space, regardless of the final shape or dimensions the element will take. The source flags this as technical work worth involving a designer on.
Add explicit width and height attributes to every image so the browser reserves space before the file arrives. Wrapping image tags in fixed-ratio containers is the equivalent modern technique.
If you run WP Rocket, enable its 'Add missing width and height attributes' image setting to apply this broadly with a single checkbox.
Re-test after each change; a single attribute fix on a large template can move the CLS score substantially.
caveats: Placeholder layout for third-party ads and embeds is genuinely technical and often needs developer or designer time.
Fix CLS before chasing other metrics on checkout — the revenue risk from mis-taps is direct.

cards.title: Reduce TBT by unblocking the main thread with JS minify, defer, and delay
cards.summary: TBT is the summed time long tasks over 50ms occupy the browser's main thread, and it is the lab metric that replaces FID for interactivity.
cards.use_when: A product or checkout page feels unresponsive on mobile — taps on add-to-cart, variant selectors, or nav menus lag — and lab data flags Total Blocking Time.
steps: Understand the mechanism: the main thread parses HTML, renders content, and processes user input. Any task running longer than 50ms is a 'long task' and blocks everything else while it runs.
TBT is the accumulated blocking from those long tasks; the source describes a failing TBT as a sign your page runs a lot of complex JavaScript.
The fastest fix per the source is to minify JavaScript files and defer or delay JavaScript execution so non-critical scripts stop occupying the main thread during load.
In WP Rocket, go to the File Optimization tab (verify current interface) and enable JS minification alone first. The plugin warns it can break things.
Save, clear the cache, and re-test the live site in an incognito window, clicking through a few pages to confirm every element renders and works.
If nothing breaks, keep it on, then repeat the same activate-save-clear-test cycle for combining JS files.
If something breaks, uncheck that single setting — the failure tells you which optimization is unsafe for your site.
Then enable deferred JS loading and delay JS execution, using the exclusion list to keep specific scripts loading first, and optionally defer plugin and theme scripts.
Re-run PageSpeed Insights to confirm TBT and the overall performance score moved.
caveats: Never enable minify/combine/defer/delay in bulk without clearing cache and testing incognito — the source's protocol exists precisely because each can break UI.
Delay JS can break interactive elements like add-to-cart or sliders if you delay scripts the page needs at first paint; exclude those.
A cached copy of the page will produce stale lab results, so clear cache before every re-test.

cards.title: Cache-bust your speed tests with an above-the-fold indicator
cards.summary: Place a visible marker above the fold and confirm it appears in the PageSpeed snapshot to prove the test ran against your updated, uncached page.
cards.use_when: Re-testing speed after editing a product page, template, or plugin setting and you need confidence the reported score reflects the new version.
steps: Before you re-run PageSpeed Insights, add a small, obvious text or element to the page — for example a temporary line reading 'test build 2' — and keep it above the fold.
Run the assessment on the live URL.
Look at the above-the-fold screenshot PageSpeed Insights renders next to the performance score.
If your indicator element appears in the snapshot, the crawl captured your latest changes and the metrics are trustworthy.
If it does not appear, your test hit a cached or stale version — clear the cache and re-run before interpreting any number.
Remove the indicator once you have confirmed the build and before you consider the page finished.
Do this on every iteration of a speed project; it prevents hours spent reacting to stale metrics.
caveats: The indicator must be above the fold or it will not appear in the rendered snapshot.
This confirms freshness of the crawl, not that the crawl matches what a real shopper's device will render.

cards.title: Use the performance score's hover hint to pick your highest-impact fix
cards.summary: PageSpeed Insights tells you which metric would most improve the performance score if fixed, so you do not have to guess the order of work.
cards.use_when: You have a long list of speed issues on a store page and limited time before a launch or campaign, and need to sequence the work.
steps: Read the overall performance score: green at 90 or above, orange from 50 to 89, red below 50 — the bands the source states.
Hover over the score indicator circle to reveal which metric would create the most impact on the score for that page.
Scroll to the optimization opportunities section, which PageSpeed Insights groups by the metric each fix affects.
Open the group matching the flagged metric first — in the source's walkthrough, TBT was the flagged area, so the TBT opportunities were the ones to work.
Work those opportunities top-down, re-testing after each change, rather than working through the whole checklist in list order.

Use the recommendations inside each opportunity as a starting point: the source notes the 'serve images in next-gen formats' item recommends converting images to WebP via a performance plugin or WP Rocket's Image Optimization tab.
Expect the score to move in jumps, not gradually — the source's example shows a WP Rocket configuration pass taking a page from 69 to 99 with nothing visibly broken.
caveats: Score movement like 69-to-99 is one demonstration on one page, not a guaranteed result for your store.
The source explicitly warns against chasing a 100 or a CrUX pass for its own sake; content depth and serving the audience are what ultimately drive rankings.
Verify the current PageSpeed Insights hover behavior and recommendation links before relying on them.

cards.title: Sequence metrics: TTFB, FCP, FID, INP and what each one actually measures
cards.summary: A shopper's page-load experience breaks into server response, first paint, click-to-processing, and click-to-visible-change — each with its own score bands.
cards.use_when: Translating a PageSpeed report into a decision about whether to change hosting, theme, plugin stack, or front-end code on a store.
steps: Time to First Byte (TTFB): time from the browser's request to the server returning the first byte. Good is below 0.8s and it should not exceed 1.8s, per the source.
First Contentful Paint (FCP): time until the first object renders, signaling to the shopper that the page is loading. Good is under 1.8s, 1.8–3.0s needs improvement, above 3.0s is poor.

First Input Delay (FID): the browser's internal processing delay between a click and starting to process it; it does not measure any visible change. Good is under 100ms, 100–300ms needs improvement, above 300ms poor. It exists only in field data.

Interaction to Next Paint (INP): the full time from interaction to the next visual change — for example an add-to-cart item visibly appearing, or a mobile menu actually opening. Good is 200ms or less, 200–500ms needs improvement, above 500ms poor.
Read the restaurant analogy: FID is the time until the waiter acknowledges your raised hand; INP is everything through to the water arriving in your glass.
When FCP is poor, the source argues the cause is usually your theme, plugins, and page elements rather than the web server — so audit the front end before buying new hosting.
Only the top three field metrics are Core Web Vitals in the current report; the rest are 'notable' or experimental, so treat them as context rather than pass/fail gates.
Verify the current report layout, as Google has shifted which metrics are labeled Core Web Vitals.
caveats: The source describes INP and FID together, but FID is field-only while INP is the broader interaction metric — do not treat them as identical.
These score bands are the source's stated thresholds; confirm against current Google documentation, since metric definitions and thresholds change.

cards.title: Speed Index and the remaining Lighthouse audits beyond performance
cards.summary: Speed Index tracks how quickly above-the-fold content becomes visible, while the accessibility, best-practices, and SEO audits cover non-speed quality checks.
cards.use_when: Running a full Lighthouse review on a product page or checkout before launch and deciding which audit failures actually matter to the store.
steps: Interpret Speed Index as how fast the above-the-fold content visually fills in. The source's view is that if the other metrics are healthy, Speed Index generally follows — so fix the underlying metrics rather than targeting Speed Index directly.
Read above-the-fold as everything visible on first load; everything else is below the fold.

Use the Accessibility audit to catch missing descriptive labels on buttons (needed by screen-reader users) and insufficient contrast between background and foreground colors — both affect real shoppers.
Use the Best Practices audit as a check on modern development standards for speed, security, and overall user experience.
Use the SEO audit to confirm structured data is valid, the page is not blocked from indexing, and a title and meta description exist — factors that help search engines index product pages.
Treat the SEO audit as a shallow check; the source notes a thorough on-page SEO checklist covers more than Lighthouse does.
caveats: The accessibility audit is a subset of real accessibility work; passing it does not make a store accessible.
The SEO audit does not assess content quality or commercial intent.

cards.title: Share a frozen PageSpeed report with your developer or agency
cards.summary: PageSpeed Insights produces a copyable link that reproduces the exact report, so speed issues can be handed off without screenshot arguments.
cards.use_when: You need a web developer or consultant to fix speed problems on a product template or checkout and want them working from the same evidence you saw.
steps: Run the assessment on the exact URL and device (mobile) you want fixed.
Click the copy-link control in the report interface (verify the current control and label).
Send the link with a short note naming the metric to fix — for example, 'TBT on the mobile product page' — rather than sending the whole report unexplained.
Instruct the recipient to open the link, which reproduces the same report rather than re-running the test on a possibly changed page.
Ask them to confirm the indicator or snapshot matches before starting, so you know they are looking at your build.
Keep the link as a record of the before state so you can compare it to the after state once fixes ship.
caveats: A stored report reflects the page at test time; if the site changes, it is a historical artifact, not a live view.
Lab data in a shared report is simulated, so do not present it to stakeholders as actual customer experience.

input.text:
08-SPD / speed and performance

Goes here. Loading performance, browser rendering, perceived performance, resource optimization, Core Web Vitals (CWV), caching strategies, and the technical mechanics of shrinking file sizes and reducing execution time. Specifically capturing the mechanical breakdown of Google PageSpeed Insights, differentiating between Field Data (CrUX) and Lab Data (Lighthouse), and outlining specific WordPress optimization settings via WP Rocket.

Topics. core web vitals / Differentiating between Field Data and Lab Data in PageSpeed Insights. Field Data (View Data): aggregated from the Chrome UX Report (CrUX) over 28 days based on real user interactions; includes First Input Delay (FID) and Interaction to Next Paint (INP). Lab Data (Lighthouse Data): simulated using a mid-tier device on a mobile network; used for immediate optimization feedback; measures Total Blocking Time (TBT) instead of FID. resource optimization / Resolving Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS): fixing dynamic content injections by using placeholders and explicitly defining image dimensions, or using the "Add missing width and height attributes" setting in WP Rocket. Resolving Total Blocking Time (TBT): reducing the time the "main thread" is occupied by tasks taking longer than 50 milliseconds. Utilizing WP Rocket's "File Optimization" tab to minify JavaScript, combine files, and defer/delay JS execution to unblock the main thread.

Look for. The definition of the Main Thread: the browser's primary worker responsible for parsing HTML, rendering content, and processing user inputs. The definition of Total Blocking Time (TBT): the accumulated time that long tasks (>50ms) prevent the main thread from responding to user interactions. The specific testing protocol when minifying/deferring JavaScript: activate the setting, clear the cache, test the live site in incognito, and uncheck if the UI breaks. The specific reason why Field Data might display "Origin" instead of "URL": the specific page tested did not receive enough traffic over the past 28 days, so PageSpeed Insights defaults to the site-wide average.

Skip. General SEO philosophy about content depth mattering more than a perfect 100 score. Plugs for the Rank Math SEO plugin or other YouTube videos. Broad explanations of accessibility or standard SEO metadata checks.
